caption:
Your body rebuilds itself faster than you think.

Sender & Milo (Nature Medicine, 2021) modelled cell turnover across every tissue. Result: roughly 330 billion cells replaced per day, about 1% of all your cells. Blood cells dominate by count (~86%), gut lining by mass share is next.

The 'every 7 years' number is a folk myth; there is no single turnover time. Neurons in the cortex mostly last a lifetime. Gut epithelium turns over in days.

Source in slide 7. Save this for the next time someone quotes the 7-year thing.

slides.title: You are not the same body you were *yesterday*
slides.sub: A 2021 Nature Medicine model counted how many cells you replace every day.

slides.title: cells replaced per day
slides.body: About *1 percent* of all the cells in your body. Roughly 80 grams of tissue.

slides.title: of that count is blood cells
slides.body: Red blood cells and neutrophils have short lives and huge numbers.

slides.myth: Every cell is replaced every 7 years
slides.body: Gut lining: days. Red blood cells: ~4 months. Fat cells: ~10 years. Most cortical neurons: your whole life.

slides.title: Three things this changes
items: **Cancer risk** tracks with division count. Tissues that divide most are where most cancers start.
**Nutrition**: ~80 g of new tissue a day needs steady protein and iron.
**Ageing** is partly the slow drift of copying errors in fast-turnover tissues.

slides.title: Your memories live in cells that never get *replaced*
slides.body: Most neurons in the cerebral cortex are as old as you are. Damage there is permanent, which is why brain injury and stroke are different from a cut.

items: Sender R, Milo R. The distribution of cellular turnover in the human body. Nature Medicine 27, 45-48 (2021).
Bianconi E et al. An estimation of the number of cells in the human body. Annals of Human Biology (2013).
slides.note: Numbers are model estimates for a reference 70 kg adult male. Percentages rounded.
